argument_summary: Certification is supportable only on a narrow basis. The admissible record shows aggregate launch readiness exceeds threshold by 2.1 percentage points and there were no severity-one rehearsal incidents. That supports a managed-release argument when paired with documented evaluations and ongoing monitoring principles. The same record also shows the small-business onboarding segment misses target by 1.3 percentage points, is named in two paid pilot commitments, and remains under open legal review. The cleanest audit treatment is therefore not to reject certification outright, but to recognize that the defense is limited to aggregate readiness and does not establish that materiality has been resolved.
claims_about_policy: The policy record cuts against a clean 'no issue' framing. The release policy says material limitations for named launch use cases must be disclosed unless resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance before launch, and the governing policy text says non-core or low-volume labels do not resolve materiality when the affected segment is named in customer commitments or legal review is pending. On this record, certification can be defended as a narrow readiness judgment, but not as proof that disclosure obligations are settled.
claims_about_business_cost: No independent business-cost claim is needed to defend the packet. The appropriate basis is the admissible readiness evidence and a bounded characterization of unresolved risk, not escalation rhetoric.
concessions: The small-business onboarding segment misses target by 1.3 percentage points.
That segment is named in two paid pilot commitments, so Product's 6% non-core characterization does not by itself resolve materiality.
Legal review is still open on whether the gap must be disclosed.
The defense for certification is weak if presented as clean compliance without caveat.
